title: Other ways of talking about the future
subtitle: on the verge of / due to / bound to
summary: Talk about what is going to happen with phrases such as on the verge of, due to, bound to and set to, and with verbs like aim, intend and propose.

lesson.heading: On the verge / brink / point of
lesson.text: Be on the verge of ... / brink of ... / point of ... (+ -ing or a noun) says that something will happen soon. Be on the brink of usually refers to something important, exciting or very bad.

examples.text: People **are on the verge of starvation** as the drought continues.
Scientists **are on the brink of making** major advances in the fight against AIDS.
Exhausted, mentally and physically, she **was on the point of collapse**.

lesson.heading: Due to, sure / bound to, set to
lesson.text: Be due to + infinitive says something is expected to happen at a particular time. Be sure to and be bound to say it is likely or certain to happen. Be set to says it is ready to happen.

examples.text: The company's chief executive **is due to** retire next year, but following today's announcement of further losses she **is sure to be** asked to leave sooner.
'Will there be somewhere to get a coffee at the station?' 'Oh, yes, **there's bound to be**.'
Her new film **is set to be** a great success.

lesson.text: Watch out for due to + noun - that gives a reason, not a future time: *Due to fog, all flights from the airport have been cancelled.*

lesson.heading: Verbs + to-infinitive for intentions
lesson.text: Many verbs take a to-infinitive to talk about intentions. Some of them can be used in the present simple or the present continuous with very little difference; the continuous is slightly more tentative.

examples.text: We **guarantee to refund** your money if you are dissatisfied with the computer.
**I aim to get** to Bangkok by the end of June.
examples.note: or I'm aiming to get ...; I was aiming to get ... is more tentative still

lesson.heading: Which verbs allow the continuous?
columns: Present simple or present continuous + to-infinitive

lesson.heading: be looking + to-infinitive
lesson.text: Some people, particularly in speech and in journalism, use be looking + to-infinitive to mean planning a course of action.

examples.text: We're **looking to create** 3,000 jobs in the city over the next year.

lesson.heading: Past forms: the future seen from the past
lesson.text: When these phrases and verbs are used with past tense forms, they usually talk about future events seen from a point in the past.

examples.text: It was his 64th birthday in 2006 and he **was due to** retire the following year.
Nathan **had resolved to** become fluent in Spanish before he left university.
The new management **had been looking to** create 20 new jobs.

lesson.heading: shall and shan't
lesson.text: Some people use shall and shan't instead of will and won't in statements about the future with I and we, although will (especially 'll) and won't are far more common. With other subjects, shall is only found in formal rules and older literary styles.

examples.text: He was a good friend and **we shall miss** him greatly.
I'm just going to buy a newspaper. **I shan't** be long.
examples.note: more commonly I won't be long

examples.text: The match referee **shall be** the sole judge of fair play.

exercises.prompt: NASA's latest Mars probe ___ to Earth later today.
exercises.explanation: Be due to + infinitive: something expected to happen at a particular time.

exercises.prompt: A spokesperson said the probe would be bringing back rock samples that are ___ exciting new information about the planet.
exercises.explanation: Be sure to + infinitive: something likely or certain to happen.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase with its meaning.

pairs.right: about to do something important, exciting or very bad
expected to happen at a particular time
certain or very likely to happen

exercises.prompt: The Countryside Conservation Society is ___ a new million-Euro scheme for the protection of endangered plant species.
exercises.explanation: Be set to + infinitive: the scheme is ready to happen.

exercises.prompt: It is estimated that over 200 species are ___ extinct in the country.
exercises.explanation: Be on the verge of is followed by an -ing form or a noun.

exercises.prompt: Sources at the United Nations have said that the governments of North and South Alicia are ___ an agreement to end their long-running border dispute.
exercises.explanation: Be on the point of + -ing: it will happen very soon.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to report what EU ministers are ready to do.
exercises.answer: EU agriculture ministers are set to make an important announcement on increasing support to farmers.
exercises.explanation: Be set to + infinitive says that something is ready to happen.

exercises.prompt: 'Many farmers are ___ out of business,' said the Italian representative, 'and the matter must be decided very soon.'
exercises.explanation: Be on the brink of is used for something very bad that is about to happen.

exercises.prompt: In the first half of the course we'll study microbiology, and in the second half I ___ with genetic engineering.
exercises.explanation: Propose takes a to-infinitive and works in the present simple or the present continuous.

exercises.prompt: Every New Year he ___ eating biscuits, but by February he has started again.
exercises.explanation: Resolve is not used in the continuous here, so the present simple is the only option.

exercises.prompt: I have passed your letter on to the manager who ___ shortly.
exercises.explanation: In current English shall is not used with other subjects to talk about the future - only will.

exercises.statement: Only people over the age of 18 shall be eligible to vote in the referendum.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Shall with other subjects is still found in formal rules, so shall or will are both possible here.
